The Intoxication of Power and the Portents of Its Downfall! — The Politics of Division versus the Pursuit of National Unity

Power, whether great or limited, can become an intoxicating experience for many. Once someone has tasted power, they are often reluctant to relinquish it. Instead, their primary concern gradually shifts towards how to retain that power and how to prolong their tenure.

This tendency is evident at the individual level, and political parties are no exception.

Once a political party assumes state power, it often becomes more preoccupied with devising strategies to remain in power than with fulfilling its responsibilities of governance. Perhaps it forgets that attaining power and becoming its permanent owner are two entirely different things. Power is never permanent for anyone. Yet, once people experience its privileges, many seem to lose sight of this simple truth.

Upon assuming power, the foremost priorities should be to strengthen national unity, reduce political divisions, and govern the country by taking along those with differing opinions and political affiliations.

Regrettably, the opposite tendency is often observed.

Instead of building national consensus, the politics of division takes precedence. Rather than bringing political opponents into the fold of mutual trust, there is a tendency to marginalize them. It appears that, after coming to power, the desire to monopolize and consolidate power becomes a greater obsession than the pursuit of national unity.

The need for national unity should be felt most strongly by the party in power. Yet, ironically, it is often the ruling party itself that initiates the politics of division. Divide and Rule seems to become its political strategy. When the very party expected to lead the process of national unity instead takes the lead in fostering division, the situation inevitably becomes a matter of serious concern.

In fact, a political party's assumption of power does not merely provide it with an opportunity to enjoy public support and implement its electoral promises; it also multiplies its responsibilities and obligations of accountability. Particularly on matters of national interest, it is a fundamental responsibility of the ruling party to build consensus by engaging all viewpoints and political stakeholders, demonstrate political tolerance, and establish an inclusive system of governance.

However, if a party, instead of fulfilling these responsibilities, becomes more preoccupied with marginalizing political opponents, suppressing dissenting opinions, or establishing exclusive control and dominance over state institutions and administrative structures, it inevitably deepens political polarization.

Such strategies may appear to the ruling party to be effective means of consolidating power, at least in the short term. But the fact that consolidating power and earning political legitimacy are not the same thing is something those in power often seem reluctant to acknowledge.

In its eagerness to retain power, a political party may push its opponents so far away that, eventually, it also loses the trust of a much broader section of the population.

In other words, those who create divisions among people in order to cling to power may ultimately find themselves alienated from the very people whose confidence they need. Over the long term, this tendency intensifies the crisis of political trust, deepens social divisions, and fuels public dissatisfaction with the government.

The very strategy employed to prolong its hold on power may ultimately undermine the political foundations of that power and pave the way for its downfall.

The success of a political party cannot be measured merely by how long it manages to remain in office. Rather, its long-term political legitimacy and success depend on how effectively it fosters national unity while in power, how tolerant it is of dissenting opinions, how successfully it strengthens democratic institutions, and how much public trust it is able to earn.

The stronger the desire to make power permanent, the greater the need to recognize the importance of public trust and political legitimacy.
